set.approach: From the South Lake trailhead, follow the Bishop Pass trail to Long Lake, cross the lake's headwaters and pick up faint paths up a shallow valley to the southwest to Margaret Lake, which is a good base for the wall. Do not climb the steep moraine toward Mt. Goode. Rather, start on the lake's north shore and contour west on faint climber paths and go up the obvious drainage right of the steep scree slope; it holds grass and granite slabs for roughly a mile before it fades into talus. Keep climbing the talus, angling right, to the point where a narrow side drainage enters from the west, and follow its floor toward the base of Trapezoid, which is easier going than the main boulder field. The wall faces east, and the routes start from the large flat ledges at the foot of the vertical green rock. Puff the Magic Dragon is the leftmost route on the face: rope up at the left end of those ledges, where the first belay bolts show up and left, about seventy feet above.
set.descent_text: Every belay on the route is bolted for rappelling, so parties descend by rappelling the line they climbed.

review.notes: Approach: area page (trailhead to talus drainage and ledges) plus route page start. Descent: route page says belays are bolted for rappel; no count given.

Do not climb the steep moraine toward Mt. Goode. Rather, start on the lake's north shore and contour west on faint climber paths and go up the obvious drainage right of the steep scree slope; it holds grass and granite slabs for roughly a mile before it fades into talus. Keep climbing the talus, angling right, to the point where a narrow side drainage enters from the west, and follow its floor toward the base of Trapezoid, which is easier going than the main boulder field. The wall faces east, and the routes start from the large flat ledges at the foot of the vertical green rock. Rasta Root starts in the middle of the face, directly below the longest splitter crack under the big overhang; look for three bolts, one clipped right off the ground for the opening thin moves.
set.descent_text: Parties rappel the route from the bolted belays. The long second-pitch crack does not reach the first belay in a single rappel, so use the separate two-bolt anchor about 25 feet to the right of that crack; from there the rope reaches the ground. Tie knots in the rope ends, especially for the rappel through the roof.

review.notes: Approach: area page plus route page start. Descent: route page rappel description (alternate anchor on the right of pitch 2).

Shield of Dreams takes the clear splitter system in the green stone on the left part of the wall, beginning from a short grey corner that faces left.
set.descent_text: Belays are bolted for rappelling, and rappelling the route is the way down. From the last pitch, a party that wants the summit moves left, still roped, to easier ground, then returns the same way to the bolts to rappel. Knot the rope ends.

review.notes: Approach: area page plus route page start. Descent: route page.

set.approach: From the South Lake trailhead, follow the Bishop Pass trail to Long Lake, cross the lake's headwaters and pick up faint paths up a shallow valley to the southwest to Margaret Lake, which is a good base for the wall. Do not climb the steep moraine toward Mt. Goode. Rather, start on the lake's north shore and contour west on faint climber paths and go up the obvious drainage right of the steep scree slope; it holds grass and granite slabs for roughly a mile before it fades into talus. Keep climbing the talus, angling right, to the point where a narrow side drainage enters from the west, and follow its floor toward the base of Trapezoid, which is easier going than the main boulder field. The wall faces east, and the routes start from the large flat ledges at the foot of the vertical green rock. Harvest Time starts roughly 150 feet left of the huge dihedral where Man on the Flying Trapezoid begins, at a conspicuous left-slanting crack in grey and white rock with one bolt ten feet off the ground.
set.descent_text: All belays are bolted, and the route can be rappelled, though the long second pitch needs a longer rope than the rest. The other option is to climb to the summit, move up and left about 150 feet to the neighbouring route's rappel anchors, which sit just below the summit and are reached by a short roped downclimb of about class 5.0, and rappel that line instead.

review.notes: Approach: area page plus route page start. Descent: route page (rappel route, or summit and use Puff anchors). Rope-length detail kept vague on purpose.

set.approach: Tendernob lies deep in the Gorge of Despair country and takes a backpack trip. The usual way in starts on Highway 180 about a mile west of Cedar Grove, climbs by the Lewis Creek trail (or the Deer Cove trail) to Frypan Meadow, then takes the west branch up to the end of the trail above Grizzly Lake. From there go cross-country toward Mt. Harrington, up a steep talus barrier, and north through the obvious notch of Harrington Pass; there is good camping with running water between the talus and the pass. Beyond the pass you pass some high tarns and reach the last alpine lake before the canyon drops into the gorge. The peak's blocky southwest face rises right there, a short walk from the lake. The route starts to the right of the big right-leaning roof that splits the face and left of the huge right-facing open book, at the toe of an arete-like bulge with cracks trending right. A wilderness permit is required to camp.

review.notes: Approach only: Gorge of Despair area page (trailhead to pass and lake), Tenderfoot Peak area page (short walk from lake), route page (start). Descent not stated by any source; none written. Distances and gain left out (single source).

set.approach: The shortest way to Whorl Mountain starts at Twin Lakes near Bridgeport and follows the trail up Horse Creek to the pass at its head. The tarns in Spiller Canyon, below the southeast face, serve as a base camp. The southeast face carries three pillars, and the Golden Pillar is the right-hand one, to the right of the third-class gully that is the standard way up. Start at the lowest toe of granite below it and scramble the rib at fourth and fifth class, soloing or short-roping, until you reach the foot of the large golden block.
set.descent_text: The route ends on a sandy slope above the last block, from which careful fifth-class scrambling leads to the middle summit of Whorl Mountain. Descend by the third-class southeast face route, the gully just left of the pillar.

review.notes: Route page: tarns, toe of pillar, scramble, SE face descent. Area page: Twin Lakes/Horse Creek Pass approach, SE face is class 3. The link between the pass and the Spiller tarns is not stated by either; kept as two separate facts.

set.approach: Whorl Mountain's north ridge begins at the low point between the middle and north peaks. One way is to scramble up directly from the east, from the hiking bench below. The other is to cross Matterhorn Pass, go up and over the north peak (some class 4 on the summit rocks), pick down the ridge, and traverse into the saddle from the west side. The climb starts from a ledge at the base of a short squeeze chimney.
set.descent_text: The last pitch finishes directly on the summit. Descend by the popular class 3-4 southeast chute, the southeast face route.

review.notes: Route page for both fields. SE face descent also confirmed as class 3 on the area page.
